{{More citations needed|date=November 2025}}{{Short description|Statistical test}}In [[statistics]], the '''Breusch–Pagan test''', developed in 1979 by [[Trevor Breusch]] and [[Adrian Pagan]],<ref name=":0">{{cite journal |last1=Breusch | first1=T. S. |author-link=Trevor Breusch |last2=Pagan |first2=A. R. |author-link2=Adrian Pagan |title=A Simple Test for Heteroskedasticity and Random Coefficient Variation |journal=[[Econometrica]] |year=1979 |volume=47 |issue=5 |pages=1287–1294 |mr=545960 |jstor=1911963 |doi=10.2307/1911963}}</ref> is used to test for [[heteroskedasticity]] in a [[linear regression]] model. It was independently suggested with some extension by [[R. Dennis Cook]] and Sanford Weisberg in 1983 ('''Cook–Weisberg test''').<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Cook |first1=R. D. |author-link=R. Dennis Cook |first2=S. |last2=Weisberg |year=1983 |title=Diagnostics for Heteroskedasticity in Regression |journal=[[Biometrika]] |volume=70 |issue=1 |pages=1–10 |doi=10.1093/biomet/70.1.1 |hdl=11299/199411 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Derived from the [[Lagrange multiplier test]] principle, it tests whether the [[variance]] of the [[errors and residuals in statistics|errors]] from a regression is dependent on the values of the independent variables. In that case, [[Homoscedasticity and heteroscedasticity|heteroskedasticity]] is present.

==Formulation==
{{Unreferenced section|date=November 2025}}
Suppose that we estimate the regression model

:<math>
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + u, \,
</math>

and obtain from this fitted model a set of values for <math>\widehat{u}</math>, the residuals. [[Ordinary least squares]] constrains these so that their mean is 0 and so, given the assumption that their variance does not depend on the [[dependent and independent variables|independent variables]], an estimate of this variance can be obtained from the average of the squared values of the residuals. If the assumption is not held to be true, a simple model might be that the variance is linearly related to independent variables. Such a model can be examined by regressing the squared residuals on the independent variables, using an auxiliary regression equation of the form
:<math>
\widehat{u}^2 = \gamma_0 + \gamma_1 x + v.\,
</math>

This is the basis of the Breusch–Pagan test.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Nguyen |first=Mike |url=https://bookdown.org/mike/data_analysis/heteroskedasticity-tests.html |title=14.3 Heteroskedasticity Tests {{!}} A Guide on Data Analysis}}</ref> It is a [[chi-squared test]]: the test statistic is distributed [[chi-squared distribution|''nχ''<sup>2</sup>]] with ''k'' degrees of freedom. If the test statistic has a p-value below an appropriate threshold (e.g. ''p''&nbsp;<&nbsp;0.05) then the [[null hypothesis]] of homoskedasticity is rejected and heteroskedasticity assumed.

If the Breusch–Pagan test shows that there is conditional heteroskedasticity, one could either use [[weighted least squares]] (if the source of heteroskedasticity is known) or use [[heteroscedasticity-consistent standard errors]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Looti |first=Mohammed |date=2025-11-06 |title=The Breusch-Pagan Test: Definition & Example |url=https://statistics.arabpsychology.com/the-breusch-pagan-test-definition-example/ |journal=Psychological Statistics |language=en}}</ref>

==Procedure==
Under the classical assumptions, ordinary least squares is the [[best linear unbiased estimator]] (BLUE), i.e., it is unbiased and efficient. It remains unbiased under heteroskedasticity, but efficiency is lost. Before deciding upon an estimation method, one may conduct the Breusch–Pagan test to examine the presence of heteroskedasticity. The Breusch–Pagan test is based on models of the type <math>\sigma_i^2 = h(z_i'\gamma)</math> for the variances of the observations where <math>z_i = (1, z_{2i}, \ldots, z_{pi})</math> explain the difference in the variances. The null hypothesis is equivalent to the <math>(p - 1)\, </math> parameter restrictions:
:<math>
\gamma_2 = \cdots = \gamma_p = 0.
</math>
The following [[Lagrange multiplier]] (LM) yields the [[test statistic]] for the Breusch–Pagan test:{{citation needed|date=June 2012}}
:<math>
\text{LM}=\left (\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\theta} \right )^{\mathsf{T}} \left (-E\left [\frac{\partial^2\ell}{\partial\theta\, \partial\theta'} \right ] \right )^{-1} \left(\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\theta} \right ).
</math>
This test can be implemented via the following three-step procedure:
* ''Step 1'': Apply OLS in the model
:: <math>
y_i = X_i\beta+\varepsilon_i, \quad i=1,\dots{},n
</math>
* ''Step 2'': Compute the regression residuals, <math>\hat{\varepsilon}_i</math>, square them, and divide by the Maximum Likelihood estimate of the error variance from the Step 1 regression, to obtain what Breusch and Pagan call <math>g_i</math>:
:: <math>
g_i = \hat{\varepsilon}_i^2 / \hat{\sigma}^2, \quad \hat{\sigma}^2 = \sum{\hat{\varepsilon}_i^2}/n
</math>
* ''Step 2'': Estimate the auxiliary regression
:: <math>
g_i=\gamma_1+\gamma_2z_{2i}+\cdots+\gamma_pz_{pi}+\eta_i.
</math>
where the ''z'' terms will typically but not necessarily be the same as the original covariates&nbsp;''x''.
* ''Step 3'': The LM test statistic is then half of the explained sum of squares from the auxiliary regression in Step 2:
:: <math>
\text{LM}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\text{TSS} - \text{RSS}\right).
</math>
where TSS is the sum of squared deviations of the <math>g_i</math> from their mean of 1, and RSS is the sum of squared residuals from the auxiliary regression. The test statistic is [[asymptotic distribution|asymptotically distributed]] as <math>\chi^2_{p - 1}</math> under the [[null hypothesis]] of homoskedasticity and normally distributed <math>\varepsilon_i</math>, as proved by Breusch and Pagan in their 1979 paper.<ref name=":0" />

== Robust variant ==

A variant of this test, robust in the case of a non-[[Gaussian]] error term, was proposed by [[Roger Koenker]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Koenker | first=Roger |author-link=Roger Koenker |title=A Note on Studentizing a Test for Heteroscedasticity |journal=[[Journal of Econometrics]] |year=1981 |volume=17 |pages=107–112 |doi=10.1016/0304-4076(81)90062-2 }}</ref> In this variant, the dependent variable in the auxiliary regression is just the squared residual from the Step 1 regression, <math>\hat{\varepsilon}_i^2</math>, and the test statistic is <math>nR^2</math> from the auxiliary regression. As Koenker notes, while the revised statistic has correct asymptotic size its [[Power of a test|power]] "may be quite poor except under idealized Gaussian conditions."<ref>{{Harvard citation|Koenker|1981|p=111}}</ref>

==Software==
In [[R (programming language)|R]], this test is performed by the function '''ncvTest''' available in the '''car''' [[R (programming language)#Packages|package]],<ref>[https://mran.microsoft.com/web/packages/car/car.pdf#page=86 MRAN: ncvTest {car}]</ref> the function '''bptest''' available in the '''lmtest''' package,<ref>[https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/lmtest/versions/0.9-36/topics/bptest R documentation about bptest]</ref><ref>{{cite book |first1=Christian |last1=Kleiber |first2=Achim |last2=Zeileis |title=Applied Econometrics with R |location=New York |publisher=Springer |year=2008 |isbn=978-0-387-77316-2 |pages=101–102 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=86rWI7WzFScC&pg=PA101 }}</ref> the function '''plmtest''' available in the '''plm''' package,<ref>[https://mran.microsoft.com/web/packages/plm/plm.pdf#page.71 MRAN: plmtest {plm}]</ref> or the function '''breusch_pagan''' available in the '''skedastic''' package.<ref>{{cite web|title=skedastic: Heteroskedasticity Diagnostics for Linear Regression Models|date=8 January 2024|url=https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/skedastic/index.html|website=cran.r-project.org}}</ref>

In Stata, one specifies the full regression, and then enters the command <code>estat hettest</code> followed by all independent variables.<ref>{{cite web |title=regress postestimation — Postestimation tools for regress |work=Stata Manual |url=https://www.stata.com/manuals15/rregresspostestimation.pdf }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |first1=A. Colin |last1=Cameron |first2=Pravin K. |last2=Trivedi |title=Microeconometrics Using Stata |edition=Revised |year=2010 |publisher=Stata Press |page=97 |isbn=9781597180481 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xPDtAAAAMAAJ&pg=PA97 |via=[[Google Books]] }}</ref>

In SAS, Breusch–Pagan can be obtained using the Proc Model option.

In [[Python (programming language)|Python]], there is a method het_breuschpagan in statsmodels.stats.diagnostic (the statsmodels package) for Breusch–Pagan test.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.statsmodels.org/stable/generated/statsmodels.stats.diagnostic.het_breuschpagan.html#statsmodels.stats.diagnostic.het_breuschpagan|title=statsmodels.stats.diagnostic.het_breuschpagan — statsmodels 0.8.0 documentation|website=www.statsmodels.org|access-date=2017-11-16}}</ref>

In [[gretl]], the command <code>modtest --breusch-pagan</code> can be applied following an OLS regression.
